extracted.intended_audience: authors and self-publishers working on book openings
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for crafting (and revising) the first sentences of a book to hook readers and avoid common, overused opening tropes. Focused on book-length fiction (and narrative nonfiction) openings for authors preparing manuscripts for publication or self-publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening lines are make-or-break
rubrics_metrics.description: Your first sentences are the make or break when it comes to convincing a reader to buy your book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page one matters to book buyers: the cover hooks them, the description signals the kind of book, and the opening lines determine what it feels like to read the book. Even if the middle of your book contains your best writing, readers won't discover it unless they get past page one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: Waking Up openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Your protagonist awakes with a start, at the sound of his/her alarm, or by someone calling their name—wakes up in any way at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trope is overdone and trite because it mirrors ordinary life; it rarely tells the reader something unique. Instead, situate readers in an environment that reveals more about your characters and plot so they become interested. If the protagonist's feeling upon waking is important, you can have them ruminate about it later rather than opening on the wake-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: Dream sequences as openings
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening scene is a dream from which your protagonist awakes later on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dream openings are worse than simple wake-ups because they can actively mislead readers—prompting investment in a dream-story that isn't the book's main plot. The advice: avoid it altogether and start where the reader can learn the most about the book's world in the most natural way possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: Literal character introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening with a character introducing themselves (e.g., 'My name is X' or direct self-introduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially common in YA, literal introductions push the reader to the periphery by telling them they're being told a story rather than allowing immersion. Use showing instead of a direct introduction: reveal the character through actions, wants, speech, or how other characters treat them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't tell in openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce us to your protagonist not by having him or her tell us who they are, but by showing what they do, what they want, what they say, or how other characters treat them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete actions, dialogue, and interactions convey character and stakes more effectively than exposition. This is given as the direct alternative to literal introductions and helps readers immerse themselves immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situate readers in an informative environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the opening in an environment that will tell the most about your characters and plot so that readers can settle in and get acclimated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than opening with generic activity (like waking), choose a scene/location/detail that reveals character, context, or conflict and makes readers curious about what will happen next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading or irrelevant openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not start with material that misleads readers about the story they will get (e.g., dream sequences that are more interesting than the actual plot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open where the book's true story and world are best and most naturally introduced; misleading openings risk losing readers who become invested in elements that won't matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite first-draft opening lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening line in your first draft is usually lazy and unoriginal—and that’s okay... but remember to go back and rewrite it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first drafts to get past the hump, then return with the aim of making the opening sharper and less trope-driven. Revision is expected and encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common/overused tropes; strive for originality
rubrics_metrics.description: If your opening feels familiar—like something you've read before—it's likely using an overdone trope and should be reworked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask yourself whether the opening feels familiar; if so, stretch creatively to find another way to tell the story. The page cites famous opening lines (Tolstoy, Austen, Dodie Smith) as examples that avoid such tropes and pull readers into the uniqueness of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to surprise and intrigue with the opening's promise
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reader picks up your book, aim to surprise and intrigue them with the promise of your opening lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening should signal a promise—something interesting or unusual that makes the reader want to continue. Use uniqueness, hook, and implied stakes rather than generic setup to create that promise.
